sentences.text: Zapalasaurus is an extinct sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous La Amarga Formation in modern-day Patagonia.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes a middle neck vertebra, a sacral fragment, 17 tail vertebrae, parts of the pelvis, and partial leg bones.
This fossil consists of a skeleton without a skull.
A femoral head diameter of 30.5 cm indicates an estimated body length of about 15 meters.
Zapalasaurus possesses unique autapomorphies, including specific neural arch structures and tail vertebrae that double in length over the first 20.
Evidence suggests that in Early Cretaceous South America, diplodocoids were at least as abundant and diverse as titanosauriforms.
Fossils of Zapalasaurus were discovered in 1995 at a site called Puesto Morales.
The specimen was excavated between 1995 and 1996 under the leadership of paleontologist José F. Bonaparte.
The holotype specimen is designated Pv-6127-MOZ.
Zapalasaurus was formally described and named in 2006 by a team led by Leonardo Salgado.
The genus name Zapalasaurus honors the city of Zapala, located about 80 km from the discovery site.
The species name bonapartei honors the Argentine paleontologist Dr. José Bonaparte.
The holotype comes from alluvial plain deposits in the upper Piedra Parada Member, representing the first fossil record for that unit.
Additional material was found in 2004.
Zapalasaurus is distinguished by features in its neck vertebrae and tail vertebrae that double in length from front to back.
Researchers assume Zapalasaurus had a long neck adapted to swing in an arc shape for feeding.
Researchers suggest Zapalasaurus likely fed at ground level.
While originally thought to be a basal diplodocoid, later analyses classify Zapalasaurus as a member of Rebbachisauridae.
Zapalasaurus was initially considered the sister group to other Diplodocoidea but is now firmly placed within Rebbachisauridae.
Zapalasaurus shares features with Rebbachisaurids, including anterior tail vertebrae with well-developed dorsal transverse process components.
Zapalasaurus lived during the Barremian and late Aptian stages of the Early Cretaceous in the Neuquén Basin.
Zapalasaurus lived between 130 and 122 million years ago in what is now South America.
The discovery of Zapalasaurus suggests that basal diplodocoid diversity in Early Cretaceous South America was greater than previously thought.
